83439.m: Under the microscope, de Mestral discovered the burrs’ hooks.

83440.q: What was George de Mestral’s job?
83440.e: George de Mestral studied engineering at a university. After that he worked as an engineer.
83440.m: George de Mestral was an engineer.

83441.q: How does a Velcro fastening hold together?
83441.e: One side has lots of small hooks, the other soft loops. When you press them together, they hook into each other.

83442.q: Roughly how long did George de Mestral work on Velcro before he applied for the patent?
83442.e: He had the idea in 1941 after an outing with his dog. He only applied for the patent in 1951, because for a long time the hooks did not hold well.
83442.m: A good invention often takes many years of work.

83443.q: In which part of Switzerland was George de Mestral born?
83443.e: He was born in 1907 in Saint-Saphorin-sur-Morges in the canton of Vaud. That is in French-speaking western Switzerland.
83443.m: George de Mestral was born in western Switzerland.

83444.q: What colour is the well-known Swiss army knife usually?
83444.e: The handle scales are usually red. They show the Swiss cross.
83444.m: The Swiss army knife is usually red.

83445.q: Which symbol is on many Swiss army knives?
83445.e: On the red handle there is an emblem with the Swiss cross. It shows where the knife comes from.
83445.m: The Swiss cross is on the pocket knife.

83446.q: Who received the first Swiss soldier’s knives in 1891?
83446.e: In 1891 the Swiss Army received its first soldier’s knife. That is where the English name Swiss Army Knife comes from.
83446.m: The pocket knife was first made for the Swiss Army.

83447.q: Who founded the well-known knife factory in Ibach?
83447.e: Karl Elsener opened a cutlery workshop in Ibach in 1884. It grew into a world-famous company.
83447.m: Karl Elsener founded the knife factory in Ibach.

83448.q: In which canton is Ibach, where pocket knives are made?
83448.e: Ibach is part of the municipality of Schwyz. Pocket knives have been made there for more than a hundred years.
83448.m: Ibach is in the canton of Schwyz.

83449.q: Why can you put a pocket knife in your trouser pocket?
83449.e: All the tools fold into the handle. That way the knife is small and the blade is protected.
83449.m: On a pocket knife, the blades fold into the handle.

83450.q: Which tool does a pocket knife often have for opening wine bottles?
83450.e: The corkscrew is a twisted spiral. You twist it into the cork and pull the cork out.
83450.m: You pull corks out of bottles with a corkscrew.

83451.q: Who was the first Swiss pocket knife made for?
83451.e: In 1891 Swiss soldiers received their first pocket knife. Later the officer’s knife with even more tools was added.
83451.m: The first Swiss pocket knife was for soldiers.

83452.q: What should children do when whittling with a pocket knife?
83452.e: If you whittle away from your body, you cannot cut yourself so easily. If the blade slips, it goes into thin air.
83452.m: Always whittle away from your body.

83453.q: What is the part you pull up and down on a zip called?
83453.e: The slider runs over the teeth. It joins them together or separates them.
83453.m: The slider opens and closes the zip.

83454.e: There are lots of small teeth on both sides. The slider presses them together so that they hook into each other.
83454.m: In a zip, small teeth interlock.

83455.q: What can happen if fabric gets caught in a zip?
83455.e: If fabric gets between the teeth, the slider cannot move on. Then you carefully pull it back.
83455.m: Fabric in a zip makes it jam.

83456.q: On which piece of clothing do you often find a long zip?
83456.e: Many jackets are closed at the front with a long zip. That is faster than with lots of buttons.

83457.q: In which country was the first forerunner of the zip invented?
83457.e: In 1893 Whitcomb Judson presented a fastener with hooks in Chicago. It was later improved into today’s zip.
83457.m: The zip has its beginnings in the USA.

83458.q: What is a zip made of?
a: Two rows of teeth and a slider
83458.e: The slider presses the teeth of the two rows into each other or separates them again. This design became established around 1913.
83458.m: In a zip, a slider joins two rows of teeth.

83459.q: What happens if a tooth of the zip is missing?
83459.e: If a tooth is missing, the teeth do not interlock properly there. The zip can burst open at that spot.
83459.m: A missing tooth can make the zip come open.

83460.q: What are the teeth of a zip often made of?
83460.e: The teeth have to be strong and small. That is why they are made of metal or plastic.
83460.m: The teeth are made of metal or plastic.

83461.q: How were letters put onto paper in old-style book printing?
83461.e: The letters were coated with ink. Then a press pushed the paper firmly onto them.
83461.m: In book printing, paper is pressed onto inked letters.

83462.q: What are the individual metal letters used in book printing called?
83462.e: Each letter was a small block of metal. Together they are called movable type.
83462.m: The letters used in book printing are called type.

83463.q: Why is the writing on a stamp back to front?
a: So it comes out the right way round on the paper
83463.e: When you stamp, the image is reversed. That is why the writing on the stamp has to be back to front. It was just the same in old-style book printing.
83463.m: The writing on a stamp is a mirror image.

83464.q: What could be made much faster thanks to book printing?
83464.e: Before that, books were laboriously copied by hand. With printing, many identical pages could be made quickly.
83464.m: Printing made books faster and cheaper to make.

83465.q: Which machine pressed the paper onto the type in book printing?
83465.e: The printing press pushed the paper evenly onto the inked type. That way every page came out clean.
83465.m: The printing press pushes the paper onto the type.

83466.q: Why could the type be used again and again in book printing?
a: It could be put together in new ways
It was carved anew each time
It was melted down after each print
The same page was always printed
83466.e: After printing, the letters were taken apart. Then they were put together into new words for the next page.
83466.m: Movable type can always be rearranged.

83467.q: Which Swiss city became an important centre of book printing early on?
83467.e: There were print shops in Basel as early as around 1470. The city became an important place for books.
83467.m: Basel was an important printing city early on.

83468.q: What was the job of the people who used to put the type together into words called?
83468.e: The typesetter put the lines together letter by letter. Only then could printing begin.
83468.m: The typesetter put the type together.

83469.q: In which city did Johannes Gutenberg live and print?
83469.e: Johannes Gutenberg was born in Mainz and had his workshop there. Mainz is on the Rhine.

83470.q: Which famous book did Johannes Gutenberg print?
83470.e: The Gutenberg Bible was made around 1454. It is one of the first large printed books in Europe.

83471.q: In which century did Johannes Gutenberg live?
83471.e: Gutenberg lived from about 1400 to 1468. That is the 15th century.
83471.m: Johannes Gutenberg lived in the 15th century.

83472.q: What did Johannes Gutenberg invent around 1450?
83472.e: Gutenberg cast individual letters from metal that could be put together again and again. That way books could be made much faster.
83472.m: Gutenberg invented printing with movable type.

83473.q: What can you see at the Gutenberg Museum in Mainz?
83473.e: At the Gutenberg Museum in Mainz you can see old printing presses and Gutenberg Bibles.
83473.m: There is a Gutenberg Museum in Mainz.

83474.q: In which country is Johannes Gutenberg’s home town today?
83474.e: Mainz is on the Rhine in Germany. There is also a monument to Gutenberg there.
83474.m: Gutenberg’s home town is in Germany today.

83475.q: Apart from books, what else did Johannes Gutenberg print?
83475.e: Gutenberg also printed small works such as a calendar for the year 1455. Newspapers, postage stamps and banknotes were only printed in Europe much later.

83476.q: What does a magnifying glass do with small things?
83476.e: Through a magnifying glass, a small object looks much bigger. That way you can make out details.
83476.m: A magnifying glass makes small things bigger.

83477.q: Why must you not leave a magnifying glass lying in the sun?
83477.e: The magnifying glass focuses sunlight onto a small spot. It can get so hot there that paper catches fire.
83477.m: A magnifying glass in the sun can start a fire.

83478.q: What can you observe well with a magnifying glass?
83478.e: A magnifying glass helps with small things that are close. For distant things you need a telescope.
83478.m: Use a magnifying glass to observe small things up close.

83479.q: Which famous detective is often shown with a magnifying glass?
83479.e: Sherlock Holmes searches for clues with a magnifying glass. That is why the magnifying glass is a symbol for detectives.
83479.m: Sherlock Holmes searches for clues with a magnifying glass.

83480.q: What is another name for a magnifier?
83480.e: A magnifier enlarges what you look at through it. That is why it is also called a magnifying glass.
83480.m: A magnifier is also called a magnifying glass.

83481.q: What happens if you hold the magnifying glass too far from the object?
83481.e: A magnifying glass only shows a sharp image at a certain distance. If it is too far away, the image becomes fuzzy.
83481.m: A magnifying glass needs the right distance for a sharp image.

83482.q: What can you use in an emergency to magnify something like a magnifying glass?
83482.e: A round drop of water works like a small lens. Letters underneath it look bigger.
83482.m: A drop of water can work like a magnifying glass.

83483.e: The lenses bend the light so that a sharp image forms in the eye.

83484.q: What are the parts of a pair of glasses that rest over the ears called?
83484.e: The arms hold the glasses in place behind the ears. That way they do not slip off your nose.
83484.m: The arms hold the glasses on your ears.

83485.q: Where do people in Switzerland usually buy glasses?
83485.e: The optician measures your eyes and fits the glasses. They also grind the right lenses.
83485.m: You get glasses from the optician.

83486.q: In which country were glasses invented more than 700 years ago?
83486.e: The first glasses were made around 1285 in northern Italy. They were reading glasses.

83487.q: Which glasses protect your eyes from strong sun?
83487.e: Good sunglasses block harmful UV light. That is especially important in the mountains and in snow.
83487.m: Sunglasses protect your eyes from strong sun.

83488.q: What do you need to see well when swimming under water?
83488.e: Diving goggles keep the water away from your eyes. With air in front of your eyes, you see clearly under water.
83488.m: With diving goggles you see well under water.

83489.q: What do you call people who cannot see clearly into the distance?
83489.e: Short-sighted people see close things well, but distant things are blurred. Glasses help them.
83489.m: Short-sighted people see distant things blurred.

83490.q: What is the best thing to clean glasses lenses with?
83490.e: Soft cloths clean the lenses without scratching them. Rough things would make scratches.
83490.m: Clean glasses lenses with a soft cloth.

83491.q: What do many people wear directly on the eye instead of glasses?
83491.e: Contact lenses are small, thin lenses. You put them directly onto the eye.
83491.m: Contact lenses sit directly on the eye.

83492.e: The Swatch is a wristwatch from Switzerland. It is especially colourful.
83492.m: The Swatch is a Swiss wristwatch.

83493.q: In which year did the first Swatch come out?
83493.e: The Swatch went on sale in Zurich on 1 March 1983.
83493.m: The first Swatch came out in 1983.

83494.q: What material is the case of the classic Swatch made of?
83494.e: The classic Swatch has a plastic case. That is why it is light and cheap.
83494.m: The classic Swatch is made of plastic.

83495.q: What was different about the Swatch compared with many other Swiss watches?
83495.e: Many Swiss watches were expensive. The Swatch was cheap, so lots of people could buy one.
83495.m: The Swatch was an affordable Swiss watch.

83496.q: In which Swiss city does the Swatch company have its headquarters?
83496.e: The company has its headquarters in Biel. Biel is an important city of the watch industry.
83496.m: The Swatch company is based in Biel.

83497.q: Which businessman is regarded as the father of the Swatch?
83497.e: From 1984, Nicolas G. Hayek made the Swatch famous all over the world. That is why he is called the father of the Swatch.
83497.m: Nicolas G. Hayek is regarded as the father of the Swatch.

a: To wake children in the morning
83498.e: Cheap watches from Asia were worrying the Swiss companies. With the affordable Swatch, they could sell lots of watches again.
83498.m: The Swatch helped the Swiss watch industry out of a crisis.

83499.q: What is the Swatch especially known for?
83499.e: There are many Swatch models in every colour. Some were designed by artists.
83499.m: The Swatch is known for its bright colours.

83500.q: Which Swiss man developed a famous milk chocolate in 1875?
83500.e: Daniel Peter mixed cocoa and sugar with milk. That was very difficult at the time, because milk contains a lot of water.
83500.m: Daniel Peter developed a famous Swiss milk chocolate.

83501.q: Why was it so difficult for Daniel Peter to mix milk into chocolate?
a: Milk contains a lot of water
83501.e: Water and cocoa butter do not mix well, and the chocolate quickly went mouldy. That is why Daniel Peter experimented for many years.
83501.m: The water in milk was the big problem with milk chocolate.

83502.q: In which town on Lake Geneva did Daniel Peter work on his milk chocolate?
83502.e: Daniel Peter had his chocolate factory in Vevey on Lake Geneva. There he developed his milk chocolate.

83503.q: Which milk did Daniel Peter use for his chocolate?
a: Goat’s milk fresh from the barn
83503.e: Daniel Peter used thickened milk with only a little water left in it. That is how he succeeded with his milk chocolate in 1875.
83503.m: Daniel Peter used condensed milk for his chocolate.

83504.q: Which neighbour in Vevey helped Daniel Peter with his experiments?
83504.e: Henri Nestlé also lived in Vevey and knew a lot about milk. He helped Daniel Peter bring his chocolate to market.
83504.m: Henri Nestlé supported Daniel Peter in his experiments.

83505.q: Which beans is chocolate made from?
83505.e: Cocoa beans grow on the cocoa tree in warm countries. They are roasted and ground.
83505.m: Chocolate is made from cocoa beans.

83506.e: The milk makes the chocolate lighter. That is why milk chocolate is light brown.

83507.q: Who invented the conche in Bern, which makes chocolate melt smoothly?
83507.e: Rodolphe Lindt invented the conche in Bern in 1879. In it, the chocolate mass is stirred for a long time and so becomes smooth.
83507.m: Rodolphe Lindt made chocolate melt smoothly.

83508.q: What happens to chocolate in the sun on a hot summer’s day?
83508.e: Chocolate melts at around body temperature. In the hot sun it becomes soft and runny.

83509.q: What do you use a peeler for?
83509.e: With the peeler you peel potatoes and carrots, for example. It only takes off a thin layer.
83509.m: A peeler peels vegetables and fruit.

83511.q: What do you use the Rex peeler for?
83511.e: With the Rex you peel potatoes, carrots or apples. The movable blade only cuts off a thin layer, so little is wasted.
83511.m: The Rex is a Swiss peeler for vegetables and fruit.

83512.q: In which year was the Rex peeler registered for a patent?
83512.e: The Rex was registered in 1947. It has looked almost the same ever since.
83512.m: The Rex peeler has existed since 1947.

83513.q: What is special about the Rex peeler?
a: The blade is crosswise and movable
83513.e: On the Rex, the blade lies crosswise to the handle and can move. That way it adapts to every curve.
83513.m: The Rex has a crosswise, movable blade.

83514.q: What material is the handle of the classic Rex peeler made of?
83514.e: The classic Rex is bent from a single piece of aluminium. It is light and does not rust.
83514.m: The classic Rex is made of aluminium.

83515.q: How did Swiss Post honour the Rex peeler?
83515.e: At the end of 2003 a 15-centime stamp showing the Rex came out. It is considered a classic of Swiss design.
83515.m: The Rex got its own postage stamp.

83516.q: Which country does the Rex peeler come from?
83516.e: The Rex was invented in Switzerland in 1947 and was made in the canton of Zurich for a long time. Today it belongs to Victorinox.
83516.m: The Rex peeler is a Swiss invention.

83517.q: What is the lead of a pencil made of?
83517.e: Despite the name, there is no lead in a pencil. The lead is made of graphite mixed with clay.
83517.m: A pencil contains graphite, not lead.

83518.q: What is the casing of a pencil usually made of?
83518.e: The lead sits inside a wooden casing. The wood protects the fragile lead.
83518.m: The casing of a pencil is usually made of wood.

83519.q: What can you use to remove pencil lines?
83519.e: The rubber rubs the graphite particles off the paper. That way the line disappears.

83520.q: What do you use to make a blunt pencil sharp again?
83520.e: A sharpener has a small blade inside. It cuts the wood and lead into a cone shape.
83520.m: You sharpen a pencil with a sharpener.

83521.q: What does the letter B on a pencil mean?
a: The lead is soft and black
The lead is hard and pale
83521.e: B stands for soft leads that write dark. H stands for hard, pale leads.
83521.m: B on a pencil means a soft, dark lead.

83522.q: Which pencil company is based in Geneva?
83522.e: Caran d’Ache has been making pencils in Geneva for more than a hundred years. The name comes from the Russian word for pencil.
83522.m: Caran d’Ache makes pencils in Geneva.

a: So they do not roll off the table
83523.e: A round pencil rolls away easily. The six edges keep the pencil on the table.
83523.m: Hexagonal pencils do not roll away so easily.

83524.q: Which hardness grade is a medium pencil for school?
83524.e: HB lies between the hard H leads and the soft B leads. That is why it is often used at school.

83526.q: What is the digit sum of the number 2026?
83526.e: You add all the digits: 2 + 0 + 2 + 6 makes 10.
83526.m: The digit sum is the sum of all the digits of a number.

83527.q: A number is divisible by 3 exactly when ... ?
a: its digit sum is divisible by 3
its first digit is divisible by 3
83527.e: You can tell divisibility by 3 from the digit sum. For 471 the digit sum is 12, so 471 is also divisible by 3.
83527.m: The digit sum is a quick check for divisibility by 3.

83528.q: How does the digit sum change if you add a zero to the end of a number?
a: It becomes ten times as big
83528.e: 47 becomes 470. In both cases the digit sum is 4 + 7, so 11, because the zero adds nothing.
83528.m: Zeros do not change the digit sum of a number.

83529.q: What is the digit sum of 999?
83529.m: With nothing but nines, the digit sum is nine times the number of digits.

83530.q: What is the repeated digit sum of 98?
83530.e: The digit sum of 98 is 17, and the digit sum of 17 is 8. You keep going until only one digit is left.
83530.m: For the repeated digit sum, you keep taking the digit sum until a single-digit number is left.

83531.q: What is the smallest natural number with a digit sum of 20?
83531.e: For the smallest possible number you need as few places as possible and digits at the end as large as possible: 2 + 9 + 9 makes 20. Two places are not enough, because 9 + 9 is only 18.
83531.m: The smallest number with a given digit sum has as many nines at the end as possible.

83532.q: The alternating digit sum is used to check divisibility by which number?
83532.e: You take the digits alternately with plus and minus, starting from the end. For 3245, 5 − 4 + 2 − 3 makes zero, so 3245 is divisible by 11.
83532.m: The alternating digit sum reveals divisibility by 11.

83533.q: The number 7_2 is divisible by 9. Which digit goes in the gap?
83533.e: The digit sum 7 + ? + 2 must be divisible by 9. That works for 9 (digit 0, number 702) and for 18 (digit 9, number 792).
83533.m: You find missing digits by completing the digit sum to fit.

83534.q: What is the digit sum of the smallest five-digit number?
83534.e: The smallest five-digit number is 10000. 1 + 0 + 0 + 0 + 0 makes 1.
83534.m: The digit sum of 10, 100, 1000 and so on is always 1.

83535.q: What is the prime factorisation of 72?
83535.e: 72 = 8 · 9, so 2 · 2 · 2 · 3 · 3. In short, you write this as 2³ · 3².
83535.m: At the end of a prime factorisation, there are only prime numbers.

83536.q: What is the prime factorisation of 100?
83536.e: 100 = 4 · 25, and 4 is 2 · 2 and 25 is 5 · 5. So 100 equals 2² · 5².
83536.m: The numbers 10, 100 and 1000 are made only of the prime factors 2 and 5.

83537.q: Which number has the prime factorisation 2 · 3 · 7?
83537.m: If you multiply all the prime factors, you get the original number back.

83538.q: In how many ways can you split the number 30 into prime factors if the order does not matter?
83538.e: 30 is always 2 · 3 · 5, however you start. Every natural number greater than 1 has exactly one prime factorisation.
83538.m: Every natural number greater than 1 can be split into prime factors in only one way.

83539.q: How many prime factors (counted with repetition) does the number 64 have?
83539.m: Powers of two are made only of the prime factor 2.

83540.q: What is the highest common factor (HCF) of 12 and 18?
83540.e: 12 = 2² · 3 and 18 = 2 · 3². They share one factor 2 and one factor 3, so the HCF is 6.
83540.m: For the HCF you take the shared prime factors.

83541.q: What is the lowest common multiple (LCM) of 4 and 6?
83541.e: 4 = 2² and 6 = 2 · 3. The LCM needs 2² and 3, so 4 · 3, which makes 12.
83541.m: For the LCM you take each prime factor in its highest power.

83542.q: What is the prime factorisation of 126?
83542.m: You keep dividing by prime numbers until only 1 is left.

83543.q: Why is the prime factorisation of large numbers important for encryption on the internet?
a: Large numbers are very hard to factorise
Large numbers have no prime factors
83543.e: Methods such as RSA rely on the fact that you can easily multiply two huge prime numbers, but can hardly split the product again.
83543.m: Factorising huge numbers is so hard that it can protect data.

83544.q: Who was Eratosthenes, after whom the famous prime number sieve is named?
a: A Greek scholar of ancient times
83544.e: Eratosthenes of Cyrene lived in the 3rd century BC and ran the famous Library of Alexandria.
83544.m: The Sieve of Eratosthenes comes from ancient Greece.

83545.q: In the Sieve of Eratosthenes, which numbers do you cross out after circling the 2?
83545.e: Every multiple of 2, so 4, 6, 8 and so on, has the factor 2 and is therefore not a prime number.
83545.m: In the sieve, you cross out the multiples of every prime you find.

83546.q: How many prime numbers are left when you use the Sieve of Eratosthenes for the numbers 1 to 100?
83546.e: Between 1 and 100 there are exactly 25 prime numbers, from 2 to 97.
83546.m: There are 25 prime numbers among the first hundred numbers.

83547.q: In the sieve up to 100, up to which prime do you have to cross out the multiples?
83547.e: You only have to check primes p where p · p is at most 100. 7 · 7 is 49, but 11 · 11 is already 121.
83547.m: You only sieve with primes whose square is not greater than the limit.

83548.q: From which number does it make sense to start crossing out the multiples of 5 in the sieve?
83548.e: The smaller multiples 10, 15 and 20 are already crossed out as multiples of 2 or 3. The first new multiple is 5 · 5, so 25.
83548.m: In the sieve, you start with the square of the prime.

83549.q: Which number is crossed out right at the start of the Sieve of Eratosthenes because it is not a prime?
83549.e: 1 has only one single factor and therefore does not count as a prime number.
83549.m: The sieve begins by crossing out the number 1.

83550.q: Which of these numbers stays in the Sieve of Eratosthenes up to 100?
83550.e: 87 = 3 · 29, 91 = 7 · 13 and 93 = 3 · 31 are crossed out. 89 has no factor except 1 and itself.
83550.m: Whatever remains in the sieve is a prime number.

83551.q: Eratosthenes is also famous for another achievement. Which one?
a: He built the first calculating machine
83551.e: Eratosthenes measured the position of the sun at two places in Egypt, Syene and Alexandria. From the difference and the distance he worked out the Earth’s circumference amazingly well.
83551.m: Eratosthenes worked out the size of the Earth more than 2000 years ago.

a: The sum of its proper factors equals the number
It is divisible by all numbers
83552.e: If you add up all the factors of a perfect number except the number itself, you get exactly the number again.
83552.m: A perfect number is as big as the sum of its proper factors.

83553.q: What is the smallest perfect number?
83553.e: The proper factors of 6 are 1, 2 and 3. Their sum is 6.
83553.m: Six is the smallest perfect number.

83554.q: What is the second smallest perfect number?
83554.e: The proper factors of 28 are 1, 2, 4, 7 and 14. Together they make 28.
83554.m: After six, 28 is the next perfect number.

83555.q: Which of these numbers is a perfect number?
83555.e: The proper factors of 496 are 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 31, 62, 124 and 248. Their sum is exactly 496.

83556.q: The proper factors of 12 are 1, 2, 3, 4 and 6. Is 12 a perfect number?
a: No, the factor sum 16 is greater than 12
Yes, the factor sum is exactly 12
No, the factor sum 10 is less than 12
83556.e: 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 6 makes 16. That is more than 12, so 12 is not perfect.
83556.m: A number is perfect only if the factor sum is exactly the number.

83557.q: What is the sum of the proper factors of 8?
83557.e: The proper factors of 8 are 1, 2 and 4. Their sum is 7, which is less than 8. So 8 is not perfect.
83557.m: For powers of two, the factor sum is always one less than the number.

83558.q: Which open question about perfect numbers is still unsolved today?
a: Whether there are odd perfect numbers
Whether perfect numbers exist at all
83558.e: All known perfect numbers are even. Nobody has yet been able to prove or disprove whether an odd one exists.
83558.m: Nobody knows to this day whether odd perfect numbers exist.

83559.q: The perfect numbers 6, 28, 496 and 8128: which digit do they end in?
83559.e: 6 and 496 end in 6, 28 and 8128 in 8. This is true of all even perfect numbers.
83559.m: Even perfect numbers always end in 6 or 8.

83560.q: Which of these numbers is a triangular number?
83560.e: 15 = 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5. You can lay 15 dots in a triangle with 5 rows.
83560.m: A triangular number is the sum of the numbers from 1 to n.

83561.e: The 10th triangular number is 1 + 2 + ... + 10, so 10 · 11 : 2, which makes 55.
83561.m: You calculate the nth triangular number as n times (n + 1) divided by 2.

83562.q: What is the sum of all the numbers from 1 to 100?
83562.e: You make pairs: 1 + 100, 2 + 99 and so on. There are 50 pairs adding up to 101, so 50 · 101, which makes 5050.
83562.m: With the pairing trick, you can add long rows of numbers in a flash.

83563.q: Which mathematician is said to have added up the numbers from 1 to 100 in a flash as a schoolboy?
83563.e: According to legend, the young Carl Friedrich Gauss found the sum in no time with the pairing trick.
83563.m: As a child, Gauss added the numbers up to 100 with a clever trick.

83564.q: What do you get when you add two consecutive triangular numbers, for example 6 and 10?
83564.e: 6 + 10 makes 16, which is 4 · 4. In the same way, 10 + 15 makes 25, which is 5 · 5.
83564.m: Two neighbouring triangular numbers always add up to a square number.

83565.q: In ten-pin bowling, the pins stand in a triangle with 4 rows. How many pins are there?
83565.e: 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 makes 10. That is the 4th triangular number.
83565.m: The ten bowling pins form the fourth triangular number.

83566.q: Which number is both a triangular number and a square number?
83566.e: 36 = 6 · 6 and at the same time 1 + 2 + ... + 8. The other numbers are square numbers but not triangular numbers.
83566.m: The number 36 is both a square and a triangular number.

83567.q: By how much does the triangular number grow when you go from the 7th to the 8th triangular number?
83567.e: The 8th triangular number has a new row of 8 dots. So 28 becomes 36.
83567.m: The nth triangular number is n more than the one before.

83568.q: A tower of tins has 6 tins at the bottom, 5 above them, then 4 and so on up to 1 tin at the very top. How many tins are there?
83568.e: 6 + 5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 makes 21. That is the 6th triangular number.
83568.m: A triangular stack always holds a triangular number of things.

83569.q: How does the Fibonacci sequence 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, ... continue?
83569.e: Each number is the sum of the two before it: 8 + 13 makes 21.
83569.m: In the Fibonacci sequence, each number is the sum of the two before it.

83570.q: In which country did the mathematician Fibonacci live?
83570.e: Fibonacci’s real name was Leonardo of Pisa, and he lived in Italy in the Middle Ages. He described the sequence in 1202 in a book on arithmetic.
83570.m: Fibonacci was a master of arithmetic from Italy.

83571.q: Which example from the animal world did Fibonacci use to explain his sequence?
83571.e: In the “Liber Abaci” he asked how many pairs of rabbits there would be after one year if every pair produced a new pair every month.
83571.m: The Fibonacci sequence began with a maths problem about rabbits.

83572.q: What is the sum of the first six Fibonacci numbers 1 + 1 + 2 + 3 + 5 + 8?
83572.e: 1 + 1 + 2 + 3 + 5 + 8 makes 20. That is exactly one less than the Fibonacci number 21, which comes two places later.
83572.m: The sum of the first Fibonacci numbers is always one less than a later Fibonacci number.

83573.q: Where in nature do you often find Fibonacci numbers?
a: In the spirals of sunflower seeds
In the number of stars in the sky
83573.e: The seeds of a sunflower form spirals whose numbers are often neighbouring Fibonacci numbers such as 34 and 55.
83573.m: Plants often arrange seeds and leaves according to Fibonacci numbers.

83574.q: Which special number does the ratio of two consecutive Fibonacci numbers get closer and closer to?
83574.e: If you divide a Fibonacci number by the one before, say 89 : 55, you get about 1.618. That is the golden ratio.
83574.m: Fibonacci numbers lead to the golden ratio.

83575.q: Which of these numbers is NOT a Fibonacci number?
83575.e: The sequence goes 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8 ... After 3 comes 5 straight away, so 4 does not appear.
83575.m: You can spot Fibonacci numbers by writing out the sequence step by step.

83576.q: A sequence works like the Fibonacci sequence but starts with 2 and 5. What is the fifth number?
83576.e: The sequence goes 2, 5, 7, 12, 19. Each number is the sum of the two before it.
83576.m: The Fibonacci rule works with any starting numbers.

83577.q: How many of the first ten Fibonacci numbers (1, 1, 2, ..., 55) are even?
83577.e: The even ones are 2, 8 and 34. In the sequence, every third number is even.
83577.m: In the Fibonacci sequence, every third number is even.

83578.q: How is a number in Pascal’s triangle made?
a: As the sum of the two numbers above it
As the product of the two numbers above it
As the difference of the neighbouring numbers
By doubling the number above it
83578.e: Every number inside is the sum of the two numbers diagonally above it. There is always a 1 at the edge.
83578.m: In Pascal’s triangle, you add the two numbers above.

83579.q: What is the row of Pascal’s triangle after 1, 3, 3, 1?
83579.e: 1 + 3 makes 4, 3 + 3 makes 6, 3 + 1 makes 4, and there is a 1 at each edge.
83579.m: Every new row starts and ends with 1.

83580.q: A unit of measurement is also named after Blaise Pascal. What is measured in pascals?
83580.e: Pressure is measured in pascals. In the weather forecast you hear about air pressure in hectopascals, for example 1013 hPa.
83580.m: Blaise Pascal gave his name to the number triangle and to the unit of pressure.

83581.q: What is the sum of all the numbers in the row 1, 4, 6, 4, 1?
83581.e: 1 + 4 + 6 + 4 + 1 makes 16. The row sums double from row to row: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16.
83581.m: The row sums in Pascal’s triangle are powers of two.

83582.q: Which numbers are in the third diagonal of Pascal’s triangle (1, 3, 6, 10, ...)?
83582.e: The diagonal 1, 3, 6, 10, 15 is made of the sums 1, 1 + 2, 1 + 2 + 3 and so on.
83582.m: The triangular numbers are hidden in Pascal’s triangle.

83583.q: Which number is in the middle of the row 1, 6, 15, ?, 15, 6, 1?
83583.e: The row above is 1, 5, 10, 10, 5, 1. The middle comes from 10 + 10, so 20.
83583.m: The rows of Pascal’s triangle are symmetrical.

83584.q: You toss a coin three times. In how many ways can you get exactly two heads?
83584.e: The row 1, 3, 3, 1 shows the number of possibilities for 0, 1, 2 and 3 heads. For two heads there are 3 ways.
83584.m: Pascal’s triangle helps you count possibilities.

83585.q: What is special about the second diagonal of Pascal’s triangle (1, 2, 3, 4, ...)?
83585.e: The outermost diagonal is made of ones. The next one counts 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and so on.
83585.m: Right next to the edge of Pascal’s triangle are the natural numbers.

83586.q: What does the pigeonhole principle say?
a: More things than boxes means one box gets at least two
Every box must be equally full
You need twice as many boxes as things
83586.e: If you share, say, 10 things among 9 boxes, at least one box must contain at least two things.
83586.m: If you have more things than boxes, at least two end up in one box.

83587.q: What is the smallest number of children a class must have so that two are sure to have their birthday in the same month?
83587.e: There are 12 months. With 12 children, each could have their own month; with the 13th child a month is sure to repeat.
83587.m: With 13 people, two are sure to share a birth month.

83588.q: There are 30 children in a class. At least how many of them have their birthday on the same day of the week this year?
83588.e: There are 7 days of the week. With at most 4 children per weekday, only 28 children would be possible. So with 30 children, at least 5 share a weekday.
83588.m: The pigeonhole principle predicts how full the fullest box must at least be.

83589.q: A drawer has black and white socks. What is the smallest number of socks you must take out in the dark to be sure of two of the same colour?
83589.e: With 2 socks, you might have one black and one white. The third sock is sure to match one of the first two.
83589.m: With two colours, three socks are enough for a certain pair.

83590.q: For a concert with 100 numbered seats, 101 tickets with seat numbers were sold by mistake. What is certain?
a: At least two tickets have the same seat number
One seat is sure to stay empty
Exactly ten seats were sold twice
83590.e: There are more tickets than seats. By the pigeonhole principle, at least two tickets must share a seat number.
83590.m: If there are more things than boxes, at least two things share a box.

83591.q: What is the smallest number of people you need so that two are sure to share a birthday (counting 29 February)?
83591.e: Including 29 February, a year has 366 possible birthdays. Only with 367 people is a repeat certain.
83591.m: One more than the number of possibilities forces a repeat.

83592.q: 25 marbles are shared among 6 boxes. At least how many marbles are in the fullest box?
83592.e: With at most 4 marbles per box, only 24 would fit. So with 25 marbles, one box must contain at least 5.
83592.m: If you divide and round up, you know the minimum in the fullest box.

83593.q: A bag holds balls in 4 colours. What is the smallest number of balls you must draw to be sure of two of the same colour?
83593.e: With 4 balls, each colour could appear exactly once. The fifth ball is sure to repeat a colour.
83593.m: With n colours you need n plus one balls for a certain pair.

83594.q: How many rods are there in the classic game “Tower of Hanoi”?
83594.e: The discs must be moved from one rod to another; the third rod is used as a helper rod.
83594.m: The Tower of Hanoi has three rods.

83595.q: Which rule applies in the Tower of Hanoi?
a: Never put a bigger disc on a smaller one
Always move two discs at once
The smallest disc may never be moved
Each disc may be moved only once
83595.e: You only ever move one disc, and a bigger disc may never lie on a smaller one.
83595.m: In the Tower of Hanoi, a big disc never lies on a smaller one.

83596.q: What is the smallest number of moves you need to move a tower of 3 discs?
83596.e: The smallest number of moves is 2 to the power of 3 minus 1, so 8 − 1, which makes 7.
83596.m: With n discs you need at least 2 to the power of n minus 1 moves.

83597.q: In the legend of the Tower of Hanoi there are 64 golden discs. What is the smallest number of moves needed?
83597.e: For n discs you need 2 to the power of n minus 1 moves. With 64 discs that is over 18 quintillion moves, far more than anyone could ever manage.
83597.m: With many discs, the Tower of Hanoi takes practically forever.

83598.q: In which country is the city of Hanoi, after which the game is named?
83598.e: Hanoi is the capital of Vietnam. The made-up legend of the game, however, tells of monks in an Indian temple.
83598.m: Hanoi is the capital of Vietnam.

83599.q: In the Tower of Hanoi, what is the smallest number of moves you need to move a tower of 4 discs?
83599.e: With 3 discs you need 7 moves. For 4 discs you first move 3 discs (7 moves), then the biggest (1 move) and then 3 discs again (7 moves): 7 + 1 + 7 makes 15.
83599.m: Each extra disc roughly doubles the number of moves.

83600.q: In the shortest solution, how often is the biggest disc moved?
83600.e: The biggest disc can only move once all the others are on the helper rod. After that it never needs to be moved again.
83600.m: In the best solution, the biggest disc moves only once.

83601.q: In the shortest solution for 3 discs, how often is the smallest disc moved?
83601.e: The smallest disc moves on every odd move, so on moves 1, 3, 5 and 7.
83601.m: In the best solution, every second move is a move of the smallest disc.

a: A puzzle in which letters stand for digits
A word that you read backwards
83602.e: You have to find out which digit each letter stands for so that the calculation works. The same letters stand for the same digits.
83602.m: In a letter sum, each letter replaces a digit.

83603.q: In the famous puzzle SEND + MORE = MONEY, which digit does M stand for?
83603.e: Two four-digit numbers make at most 19998. So the fifth place of MONEY can only be a carry of 1.
83603.m: When adding two numbers, a carry into a new place is always 1.

83604.q: In the puzzle SEND + MORE = MONEY, which letter stands for the digit 0?
83604.e: In the thousands place, S + M with a carry gives a number that starts with M again. That only works with S equal to 9, and then only the digit 0 is left for O.
83604.m: In the puzzle with SEND, MORE and MONEY, O stands for zero.

83605.q: Solve the letter sum A + A = 8. Which digit is A?
83605.e: 4 + 4 makes 8. The same letters always stand for the same digit.
83605.m: In letter sums, the same letters stand for the same digits.

83606.q: Solve the letter sum A + A + A = BA. Which digit is A?
83606.e: 5 + 5 + 5 = 15, so A is 5 and B is 1. No other digit fits.
83606.m: In letter sums, you try out all the possible digits systematically.

83607.q: Solve the letter sum AB + B = BA. Which number is AB?
83607.e: 89 + 9 makes 98. The digits are swapped, so AB = 89 is right.
83607.m: With swapped digits, looking at the ones place helps.

83608.q: Solve the letter sum AA + B = BCC. Which digit does C stand for?
83608.e: A two-digit number plus a one-digit number only gives a three-digit number if 99 + 1 = 100. So C is 0.
83608.m: A three-digit sum of such small numbers always starts with 1.

83609.q: The letter sum A · A = 2A has exactly one solution (2A is a two-digit number with tens digit 2). Which digit is A?
83609.e: 5 · 5 makes 25. The tens digit is 2 and the ones digit is 5 again.
83609.m: Squares that end in the same digit are a good clue.

83610.q: Which two truth values does classical logic know?
83610.e: In classical logic, every statement is either true or false.
83610.m: In classical logic, every statement has the truth value true or false.

83611.q: What is the truth value of the statement “7 is an even number”?
83611.e: 7 is not divisible by 2 and is therefore odd. So the statement is false.
83611.m: A statement is false if it does not match the facts.

83612.q: When is an “and” statement (“A and B”) true?
a: Only if A and B are both true
If at least one is true
83612.e: “Bern is in Switzerland and 2 + 2 makes 5” is false, because the second part is false.
83612.m: An “and” statement is true only if both parts are true.

83613.q: When is an “or” statement (“A or B”) true in logic?
a: If at least one part is true
Only if exactly one part is true
83613.e: The logical or is inclusive. “3 is odd or 4 is even” is true, even though both parts are true.
83613.m: A logical or is true as soon as one part is true.

83614.q: Statement A is true. What is the truth value of “not A”?
83614.e: Negation reverses the truth value. True becomes false and false becomes true.

83615.q: Which of these sentences has no truth value?
83615.e: A question claims nothing and is therefore neither true nor false. Only statements have a truth value.
83615.m: Only statements, not questions, are true or false.

83616.q: How many rows does a truth table for two statements A and B have?
83616.e: A and B can each be true or false. That gives 2 · 2, so 4 combinations.
83616.m: With each extra statement, the number of rows in a truth table doubles.

83617.q: On an island, knights always tell the truth and knaves always lie. Someone says: “I am a knight.” What do you know for certain?
83617.e: A knight says it because it is true, and a knave says it because he is lying. So the statement gives nothing away.
83617.m: Some statements do not help at all in solving a logic puzzle.

83618.q: Think of a number, double it, add 10, halve the result and take away the number you thought of. What do you always get?
83618.e: x becomes 2x + 10, halved x + 5. If you take away x, 5 is always left.
83618.m: Many number tricks work because the number you thought of cancels out at the end.

83619.q: You write a three-digit number twice in a row, for example 347347. Which number is the result always divisible by?
83619.e: 347347 equals 347 · 1001. This is true for every three-digit number, so the result is always divisible by 7, 11 and 13.
83619.m: A doubled three-digit number is always a multiple of 1001.

83620.q: Which trick do you use to work out 23 · 11 in your head?
83620.e: The middle digit is the sum of the two digits: 2, 5, 3 gives 253. That is right, because 230 + 23 is 253.
83620.m: In the times-11 trick, you put the sum of the digits in the middle.

83621.q: What is 35 · 35 using the trick “tens digit times the next number, then add 25 on the end”?
83621.e: 3 · 4 makes 12; then you add 25 on the end and get 1225.
83621.m: Squares of numbers ending in 5 always end in 25.

83622.q: In the 1089 trick, you take a three-digit number whose first and last digits differ by at least 2 and subtract its reverse (smaller from larger). You add the reverse of the result to the result. What do you get?
83622.e: Example: 732 − 237 makes 495, and 495 + 594 makes 1089. It works with every suitable starting number.
83622.m: The 1089 trick always leads to the same result.

83623.e: 37 · 3 makes 111. So 37 · 6 gives the number 222 and 37 · 9 gives 333.
83623.m: With 37 you get numbers with repeated digits.

83624.e: 12345679 · 9 makes 111111111. The number 12345679 deliberately has no 8.
83624.m: Some multiplications surprisingly give nothing but ones.

83625.q: You arrange the digits of a four-digit number in descending and ascending order and subtract the smaller number from the larger. If you repeat this, which number do you end up at?
83625.e: This number is called Kaprekar’s constant. It works for all four-digit numbers whose digits are not all the same, after at most seven steps.
83625.m: Kaprekar’s constant 6174 is the goal of a famous number trick.

83626.q: You count how many bikes are in front of the school. What are you doing?
83626.e: When you count, measure or ask and write down the result, you are collecting data.
83626.m: Counting and writing it down means collecting data.

83627.q: What is the easiest way to count how many red cars drive past?
83627.e: For each red car you draw a line. At the end you count the lines.
83627.m: With a tally chart you can count quickly and easily.

83628.q: How do you write the number 5 on a tally chart?
a: Four lines and one line across
83628.e: You draw four lines and cross them through with the fifth line. That makes bundles of five.
83628.m: On a tally chart you always bundle five lines.

83629.q: A tally chart shows two bundles of five and three lines. How many is that?
83629.e: Two bundles of five are 10, plus 3 lines. 10 + 3 makes 13.
83629.m: Bundles of five help you add up quickly.

83630.q: What is best for measuring how tall a plant is?
83630.e: You measure lengths with a ruler or tape measure. Then you write down the number.
83630.m: To collect data you need the right measuring tool.

83631.q: What do you use to collect data about the weather, for example the temperature?
83631.e: A thermometer shows how warm or cold it is. You can write down the reading every day.

83632.q: Why do you write down data you have collected?
a: So you do not forget it
83632.e: What you write down you can read again later, compare and analyse.
83632.m: Data that is written down can be looked at again later.

83633.q: Every day you check whether the sun is shining. How long should you do this to get a good overview?
83633.e: The longer you observe, the more data you have. Then you see whether it is often or rarely sunny.

83634.q: Where do you enter numbers you have collected so they are clear?
83634.e: A table has rows and columns. That way you can find each number again quickly.
83634.m: In a table, data stands neatly in rows and columns.

83635.q: What do you write down before you go shopping?
83635.e: On a shopping list you write one below the other what you want to buy. That way you do not forget anything.
83635.m: A shopping list helps you not to forget anything.

83636.q: How are things usually written on a list?
a: Drawn on top of each other
83636.e: On a list you write each item on its own line, one below the other.
83636.m: On a list each item has its own line.

83637.q: What do you call a single thing on a list?
83637.e: Each thing written on the list is an item.
83637.m: A list is made up of single items.

83638.q: Your shopping list has bread, milk, cheese and apples. How many items are there?
83638.e: Bread, milk, cheese and apples are four things, so four items.
83638.m: You can count the items on a list.

83639.q: What do you do with an item on your to-do list when the task is done?
83639.e: With a tick you see straight away what is already done and what is still missing.
83639.m: You tick off finished tasks on the list.

83640.q: Which list shows which children are in the class?
83640.e: The class list has the names of all the children in a class.
83640.m: The class list names all the children in a class.

83641.q: You have a list with 6 names and cross out 2. How many names are left?
83641.e: 6 minus 2 makes 4. Four names are not crossed out yet.

83642.q: What is on a guest list for a party?
83642.e: A guest list shows who is invited to the party.
83642.m: The guest list has all the invited guests.

83643.q: Why do you number the items on a list 1, 2, 3 and so on?
83643.e: With numbers you see straight away how many items there are, and you can name each one exactly.

83644.q: Which name comes first in alphabetical order: Lea, Ben or Mia?
83644.e: You look at the first letter. B comes before L and M.
83644.m: When sorting alphabetically, the first letter counts first.

83646.q: Which letter comes directly before F in the alphabet?
83646.e: The order is C, D, E, F, G. So E comes before F.
83646.m: If you know the alphabet well, you find neighbouring letters quickly.

83647.q: How many letters does the alphabet have?
83647.e: The alphabet goes from A to Z and has 26 letters.

83648.q: Which letter comes directly after M in the alphabet?
83648.e: The order is K, L, M, N, O. So N comes after M.
83648.m: You need to know the alphabet by heart to sort well.

83649.q: Which city comes last in alphabetical order: Bern, Zurich or Lucerne?
83649.e: Z is the last letter of the alphabet. That is why Zurich comes after Bern and Lucerne.
83649.m: Words with Z come right at the end.

83652.q: You have buttons in red, blue and yellow. How can you group them?
83652.e: All the red buttons go together, and so do all the blue and all the yellow ones.
83652.m: When grouping, things that have something in common go together.

83653.q: Which thing does not fit in the group: apple, pear, banana, hammer?
83653.e: Apple, pear and banana are fruit. A hammer is a tool.
83653.m: When you group things, you also see what does not belong.

83654.q: What do a dog, a cat and a rabbit have in common?
83654.e: Dog, cat and rabbit all belong to the group of animals.
83654.m: Things in a group share a feature.

83655.q: You have 12 children and make groups of 3. How many groups are there?
83655.e: 12 divided into groups of 3 makes 4 groups, because 4 · 3 makes 12.
83655.m: To share into equal groups you divide.

83656.q: How can you group building blocks?
83656.e: You can sort building blocks into cubes, cuboids and cylinders, for example.
83656.m: Shapes, colours and sizes are good for grouping.

83657.e: Bike, bus and train are all vehicles. Each of the other groups has something else in it.
83657.m: In a group, all the things go together.

83658.q: When you sort things into groups, what becomes easier?
83658.e: If you know which group something is in, you find it more quickly.

83659.q: Which animal does not fit with the others: eagle, sparrow, blackbird, trout?
83659.e: Eagle, sparrow and blackbird are birds. The trout is a fish.

83660.q: What does a Venn diagram show?
83660.e: In a Venn diagram you draw circles. Into each circle go the things that belong to the same set.
83660.m: A Venn diagram shows groups as circles.

83661.q: How do you usually draw a set in a Venn diagram?
83661.e: A closed line like a circle surrounds all the things that belong to the set.
83661.m: You draw a set with a closed line.

83662.q: One circle is called “red”, another “round”. Where does a red ball go?
83662.e: A red ball is red and round. That is why it belongs in both circles, so in the shared part.
83662.m: Something that belongs to two sets goes in the overlap.

83663.q: A circle is called “animals”. Where does a stone go?
83663.e: A stone is not an animal. That is why it does not belong in the circle “animals”.
83663.m: Something that does not belong to the set goes outside.

83664.q: Circles “can fly” and “has feathers”: where does a duck go?
83664.e: A duck can fly and has feathers. So it goes in the shared part of the two circles.
83664.m: One thing can be in several sets at the same time.

83665.q: Circles “can fly” and “has feathers”: where does a penguin go?
83665.e: A penguin has feathers but cannot fly. That is why it goes only in the circle “has feathers”.

83666.q: The circle “even numbers” contains 2, 4 and 6. Where does 8 go?
83666.e: 8 is an even number, just like 2, 4 and 6. So it goes in the circle.
83666.m: Numbers can also be sorted into sets.

83667.q: The circle “children with a bike” has 5 children, the circle “children with a scooter” has 4. Two children are in both circles. How many children have a bike but no scooter?
83667.e: Of the 5 children with a bike, 2 also have a scooter. 5 minus 2 makes 3.
83667.m: You have to pay attention to the overlap when counting.

83668.q: What does a family tree show?
83668.e: A family tree shows the family: parents, children, grandparents and so on.
83668.m: A family tree shows how a family is related.

83669.q: What do you call your parents' parents?
83669.e: The mother and father of your mother or father are your grandparents.
83669.m: Your parents' parents are your grandparents.

83670.q: What do you call children with the same parents?
83670.m: Brothers and sisters are called siblings.

83671.e: The children of your aunt and uncle are your cousins.
83671.m: The children of your uncle and aunt are your cousins.

83672.q: How many grandparents does a person have?
83672.e: Every person has two parents, and each parent has two parents too. 2 + 2 makes 4.

83673.e: Your parents' sisters are your aunts.
83673.m: Your mother's or father's sister is an aunt.

83674.q: Where in a family tree are the oldest relatives often shown?
83674.e: Often the oldest are at the top and the younger family members below. But some family trees are drawn the other way round.
83674.m: A family tree arranges the family by generations.

83675.q: What do you call the children of your children?
83675.e: For grandparents, the children of their children are their grandchildren.
83675.m: The children of your own children are your grandchildren.

83676.q: What do you need a dictionary for?
a: To look up how to spell a word
83676.e: In a dictionary you find the correct spelling and often the meaning of words too.
83676.m: You look up words in a dictionary.

83677.q: You are looking up “zebra” in a dictionary. Where do you look?
83677.e: Z is the last letter of the alphabet. That is why words with Z are right at the back.
83677.m: You find words with Z at the back of the dictionary.

83678.q: You are looking up “ant” in a dictionary. Where do you look?
83678.e: A is the first letter of the alphabet. Words with A are at the beginning.
83678.m: You find words with A at the front of the dictionary.

83679.q: What are the words at the top of a dictionary page for?
a: They show which words are on the page
They show the colour of the page
83679.e: At the top there is often the first or last word on the page. That way you quickly see whether the word you want is on this page.
83679.m: The guide words at the top show which words are on a page.

83680.q: You are looking for “cat”. The page starts with “camel” and ends with “canoe”. What do you do?
83680.e: In “cat”, t comes after n. So “cat” comes after “canoe”, further back in the dictionary.
83680.m: When looking things up, you compare letter by letter.

83681.q: In which form do you usually find “went” in the dictionary?
83681.e: Verbs are usually listed in their basic form in the dictionary. So for “went” you look up “go”.
83681.m: You look up verbs in the dictionary in their basic form.

83682.q: In which form do you usually find “mice” in the dictionary?
83682.e: Nouns are listed in the singular in the dictionary. For “mice” you look up “mouse”.
83682.m: You look up nouns in the dictionary in the singular.

83683.q: What is the name of a well-known German dictionary that is also used in Swiss schools?
83683.e: The Duden is a well-known dictionary for German spelling.
83683.m: The Duden shows the correct spelling of German words.

a: A list of all the books in the library
83684.e: The catalogue shows which books the library has and where they are.
83684.m: In the library catalogue you find all the books in a library.

83685.q: What can you search for in the library catalogue?
83685.e: You can search by the title of the book, the name of the author or a topic.
83685.m: In the catalogue you search by title, author or topic.

83686.q: What do you usually need to borrow a book from the library?
83686.e: With the card, the library knows who has borrowed the book.
83686.m: You borrow books with a library card.

83687.q: What is the small sticker with letters and numbers on the spine of a book, which shows where the book belongs, called?
83687.e: The shelf mark is like an address. It shows which shelf the book belongs on.
83687.m: The shelf mark shows a book's place on the shelf.

83688.q: How do many libraries search their catalogue today?
83688.e: In the past there were index cards in drawers. Today the catalogue is usually stored on a computer.
83688.m: Today the library catalogue is usually on the computer.

83689.q: What must you do when the loan period of a book is over?
83689.e: Borrowed books belong to the library. After the loan period you take them back so that others can read them too.
83689.m: You return borrowed books on time.

83690.q: What does the catalogue show when a book is currently on loan?
a: That it is not on the shelf
83690.e: The catalogue shows whether a book is available or currently on loan.
83690.m: The catalogue tells you whether a book is there right now.

83691.q: Before there were computers, where was the information about the books written?
83691.e: There was an index card for each book. The cards were kept in order in drawers.
83691.m: In the past a library catalogue was made of lots of index cards.

83692.q: Why do you stick a label on a box?
a: So you know what is inside
83692.e: The label says what is in the box. That way you do not have to open it.
83692.m: A label shows what is in a box.

83693.q: What is often written on the label on your exercise book?
83693.e: With your name and the subject, everyone knows straight away whose book it is and what it is for.
83693.m: The label on an exercise book shows name and subject.

83694.q: What is on the label of a yoghurt in the shop?
a: The use-by date and the ingredients
83694.e: Food packaging shows, for example, the ingredients and when you should eat it by.
83694.m: Labels in the shop show important information about the goods.

83695.q: A jar says “Sugar”, but there is salt inside. What is wrong?
83695.e: A label must match what is inside. Otherwise it is misleading.
83695.m: A label must always match what is inside.

83696.q: What does the label in your T-shirt often show?
83696.e: The label in clothes shows, for example, the size and how to wash them.
83696.m: Clothes labels show size and care.

83697.q: The boxes in the classroom have labels: “Pens”, “Scissors”, “Glue”. Where do you put a pair of scissors?
83697.e: The label shows what belongs in the box. Scissors belong in the box “Scissors”.
83697.m: Labels help you put things away in the right place.

83698.q: What on a label helps children who cannot read yet?
83698.e: A picture, for example of a pen, shows what is in the box even without reading.
83698.m: You can understand pictures on labels without reading.

83699.q: What is on a label on a suitcase at the airport?
a: Where the suitcase is travelling to
83699.e: The luggage label shows the destination. That way the suitcase is loaded onto the right plane.
83699.m: A luggage label gets the suitcase to the right destination.

83700.q: Which category does the tulip belong to?
83700.e: The tulip is a flower. That is why it belongs to the category flowers.
83700.m: A category groups similar things under one name.

83701.q: Which category does the guitar belong to?
83701.e: You make music with a guitar. It belongs to the musical instruments.
83701.m: Musical instruments form their own category.

83702.q: Which word is the name of a category?
83702.e: Carrot, leek and pea are single things. Vegetables is the general term, so the category.
83702.m: The name of a category is a general term.

83703.e: You put on a jumper. Plate, scissors and spoon are not clothes.
83703.m: Clothes are everything you put on.

83704.q: What does NOT belong in the category “furniture”?
83704.e: Table, chair and wardrobe are furniture. A banana is a fruit.
83704.m: Not everything fits into every category.

83705.q: In which category do you find a book about dinosaurs in the library?
83705.e: A book that explains real facts about dinosaurs is a non-fiction book.
83705.m: Books with real facts belong to non-fiction.

83706.q: Which category does orange juice belong to?
83706.e: You drink orange juice. That is why it belongs to drinks.
83706.m: Everything you drink belongs to the category drinks.

83707.q: Why are there categories in the shop like “bread”, “dairy” or “vegetables”?
83707.e: When similar goods are together, you know where to look.
83707.m: Categories help you find things quickly.

83708.q: What is in a fact file about an animal?
a: Important facts like size and food
83708.e: A fact file contains short, important facts, for example name, size, habitat and food.
83708.m: A fact file sums up important facts briefly.

83709.q: What belongs in a fact file about you?
83709.e: A personal fact file has details like name, age, hobbies and favourite food.
83709.m: A fact file about you has your name and age.

83710.q: How are the facts in a fact file usually written?
83710.e: You should be able to read a fact file quickly. That is why you write short key words one below the other.
83710.m: A fact file is short and clear.

83711.q: Which fact fits under “Food” in a squirrel's fact file?
83711.e: Squirrels like to eat nuts, seeds and buds. The other words describe something else, for example the colour or the size.
83711.m: Each fact belongs under the right heading.

83712.q: What is often shown on a fact file as well?
83712.e: A photo or drawing shows straight away what the animal or person looks like.
83712.m: A picture makes a fact file clearer.

83713.q: Which detail should you NOT write in a fact file that is on the internet?
83713.e: Your address is private. Strangers should not know where you live.
83713.m: Private details like my address do not belong on the internet.

83714.q: A fact file says: “lives in water, has fins, breathes with gills”. Which animal is it?
83714.e: Fish have fins and gills. With them they can swim and breathe in water.
83714.m: With a good fact file you can recognise an animal.

83715.q: Under which heading in an animal fact file does “forest” go?
83715.e: The habitat says where an animal lives, for example in the forest, in water or in a meadow.
83715.m: The habitat shows where an animal is at home.

83716.q: In the past, what did the police use wanted posters describing a person for?
a: To find people they were looking for
83716.e: In the past the police searched for people with wanted posters. They showed what the person looked like and their features.
83716.m: A description like this lets people recognise someone.

83717.q: What do you do in a survey?
a: Ask lots of people the same thing
Read a book on your own
83717.e: In a survey you ask several people the same question and collect the answers.
83717.m: In a survey you ask lots of people the same thing.

83718.q: Which question is good for a survey in the class?
a: How many legs does a dog have?
83718.e: With this question, each child gives a different answer. The other questions have only one correct answer.
83718.m: A good survey question can be answered in different ways.

83719.q: In a survey, 8 children say “pizza”, 5 “spaghetti” and 3 “soup”. What is the most popular?
83719.e: Pizza has the most answers, with 8 votes.
83719.m: The answer with the most votes is the most popular.

83720.q: In a survey, 8 children say “pizza”, 5 “spaghetti” and 3 “soup”. How many children were asked?
83720.e: 8 + 5 + 3 makes 16. That is how many children answered.
83720.m: If you add up all the answers, you know how many took part.

83721.q: What is a good way to show the results of a survey?
83721.e: In a bar chart each bar is as tall as the number of votes. That way you see straight away what is most common.
83721.m: A bar chart shows survey results at a glance.

83722.q: What is important in a survey?
a: You only ask your best friends
Whoever answers first gets two votes
83722.e: If someone counts more than once or only friends are asked, the result is no longer right.
83722.m: In a fair survey each vote counts only once.

83723.q: In a survey, the bars are 6 for “cat” and 9 for “dog”. How many more votes does “dog” have?
83723.e: 9 minus 6 makes 3. So the dog has 3 more votes.
83723.m: You find differences in a chart by subtracting.

83724.q: What must you NOT do in a survey?
83724.e: The answers must stay exactly as people gave them. Otherwise the survey is wrong.
83724.m: You always report survey answers honestly.

83725.q: How can you vote quickly in a class survey?
a: You send each child a letter
83725.e: Everyone who chooses an answer raises their hand. Then you count the hands.
83725.m: You can vote quickly by raising your hand.

83726.q: What colour is the star of the edelweiss?
83726.e: The star of the edelweiss is made of white, felty bracts. Small yellowish flower heads sit in the middle.
83726.m: The edelweiss has a white star.

83727.e: Edelweiss is thickly covered in fine white hairs. That is why it feels like soft felt.
83727.m: Edelweiss feels as soft as felt.

83728.q: What are the many fine hairs on the edelweiss for?
83728.e: High in the mountains the sun is strong and the nights are cold. The thick coat of hairs protects the plant against this and helps stop it drying out.
83728.m: The hairs protect the edelweiss like a warm fur coat.

83729.q: Can you simply pick edelweiss in Switzerland?
a: Yes, as much as you like.
83729.e: Edelweiss is protected in Switzerland. You can look at it and take photos, but you should leave it where it is.
83729.m: Leave protected flowers where they are.

83730.q: Where does edelweiss like to grow best?
a: on rocks high in the mountains
on the shore of a lake
in a field in the valley
83730.e: Edelweiss grows on stony grassland and on rocks, often on limestone. You usually find it high up in the mountains.
83730.m: Edelweiss lives high up among the rocks.

83731.q: Many Swiss wrestlers wear a blue shirt with white flowers on it. Which flower is it?
83731.e: The blue edelweiss shirt is part of the traditional dress of alpine herdsmen and Swiss wrestlers. The edelweiss is a symbol of the Alps.
83731.m: The edelweiss is a flower that stands for the Alps.

83732.q: Translated, the scientific name of the edelweiss means …?
83732.e: The name “Leontopodium” comes from Greek: “leon” means lion and “podion” little foot. The felty flowers remind people of a little paw.
83732.m: In Greek the edelweiss is called little lion’s foot.

83733.q: In which season does edelweiss flower?
83733.e: Edelweiss flowers from about July to September. Before that there is often still snow in the mountains.

83734.q: What colour is the trumpet gentian?
83734.e: The trumpet gentian has big, deep blue flowers. They sit almost directly on the ground.
83734.m: The trumpet gentian is deep blue.

83735.q: What shape are the big flowers of the trumpet gentian?
83735.e: The flowers of the trumpet gentian are big and shaped like a funnel or a bell. They can be up to 5 centimetres long.
83735.m: The gentian has flowers like blue bells.

83736.q: What does the gentian do when it gets cold or rains?
a: It pulls back into the ground.
83736.e: When it is cold and there is little light, the gentian closes its flowers. That way its pollen and nectar stay protected.
83736.m: In bad weather the gentian closes its flowers.

83737.q: How tall can the great yellow gentian grow?
83737.e: The great yellow gentian is a sturdy perennial. It usually grows 50 to 140 centimetres tall.
83737.m: The great yellow gentian is a giant among gentians.

83738.q: Which part of the great yellow gentian is dug up to make medicine?
83738.e: The great yellow gentian has a thick, long root. Remedies that are meant to help the stomach are made from it.
83738.m: With the great yellow gentian, the root is used.

83739.q: What does the root of the great yellow gentian taste like?
83739.e: Gentian root contains bitter substances. They are among the most bitter plant substances known.

83740.q: What shape are the flowers of the small spring gentian?
83740.e: The spring gentian has small, bright blue flowers. The five tips stand open like a star.
83740.m: The spring gentian has blue star-shaped flowers.

83741.q: What is a strong, deep blue named after an alpine flower called?
83741.e: The flowers of many gentians are a strong dark blue. That is why people speak of “gentian blue”.
83741.m: A deep blue is also called gentian blue.

83742.q: Which insect often crawls deep into the bell of a gentian flower?
83742.e: Bumblebees are strong and can crawl deep into the bell. There they get nectar and pollinate the flower.

83743.q: Is the alpenrose a real rose?
83743.e: The alpenrose only takes its name from the rose. In fact it belongs to the rhododendrons and the heather family.
83743.m: The alpenrose is not a real rose.

83744.q: What colour are the flowers of the alpenrose?
83744.e: The alpenrose flowers in bright pink to red. In summer it turns whole slopes red.
83744.m: The alpenrose flowers pink to red.

83745.e: The alpenrose is a shrub. It usually grows 50 to 100 centimetres tall.
83745.m: The alpenrose is a small shrub.

83746.q: What happens to the leaves of the alpenrose in winter?
83746.e: The alpenrose is evergreen. Its leathery leaves stay on the shrub in winter too, often under the snow.
83746.m: The alpenrose keeps its leaves in winter.

83747.q: Can you eat the leaves of the alpenrose?
83747.e: All parts of the alpenrose are poisonous. So you must not eat them.

83748.q: What colour is the underside of the leaves of the rusty-leaved alpenrose?
83748.e: Lots of small rusty brown scales sit on the underside of the leaves. That is how this alpenrose got its name.
83748.m: The rusty-leaved alpenrose is rusty brown underneath.

83749.q: How can you recognise the hairy alpenrose?
a: by fine hairs on the edge of the leaves
83749.e: The hairy alpenrose has fine hairs like eyelashes on the edge of its leaves. It likes to grow on limestone.
83749.m: The hairy alpenrose has eyelashes on the edge of its leaves.

83750.q: In which months does the alpenrose usually flower?
83750.e: The alpenrose flowers in early summer, usually in June and July. The higher up it grows, the later it flowers.
83750.m: The alpenrose flowers in early summer.

83751.q: What colour is the black vanilla orchid?
83751.e: The black vanilla orchid has dark reddish brown flowers. From far away it looks almost black, which is why its German name means “little coal rose”.
83751.m: The black vanilla orchid is as dark as coal.

83752.q: What does the black vanilla orchid smell of?
83752.e: The small flowers of the black vanilla orchid smell strongly of vanilla. Some people think it smells like chocolate.
83752.m: The black vanilla orchid smells of vanilla.

83753.q: Which plant family does the black vanilla orchid belong to?
83753.e: The black vanilla orchid is a small orchid. In the Alps many orchids grow in mountain meadows.
83753.m: The black vanilla orchid is an orchid.

83754.q: What shape is the flower head of the black vanilla orchid?
83754.e: Lots of tiny flowers sit close together. They form a small, round to cone-shaped head.
83754.m: The black vanilla orchid has many flowers in one head.

83755.q: About how tall does the black vanilla orchid grow?
83755.e: The black vanilla orchid is a small plant. It usually grows only about 10 to 20 centimetres tall.
83755.m: The black vanilla orchid is a small flower.

83756.q: Where does the black vanilla orchid grow?
a: in mountain meadows and alpine pastures
83756.e: The black vanilla orchid grows in sunny mountain meadows and pastures. It flowers there in summer.
83756.m: The black vanilla orchid grows in mountain meadows.

83757.q: Why shouldn’t you pick the black vanilla orchid?
a: It is an orchid and protected in many places.
83757.e: The black vanilla orchid is a small orchid. Orchids are protected in many cantons, so you leave them standing.

83758.q: What colour are the outer petals of the alpine aster?
83758.e: The alpine aster has a ring of purple petals. It shines between stones and grass.

83759.q: What colour is the middle of the alpine aster?
83759.e: Lots of small yellow flowers sit in the middle of the alpine aster. The purple petals stand around the outside.
83759.m: The alpine aster has a yellow middle.

83760.q: How many flower heads does an alpine aster stem usually have?
83760.e: Each alpine aster stem usually has only one single flower head. It is about 3 to 5 centimetres across.
83760.m: The alpine aster usually has one head per stem.

83761.q: Where does the alpine aster like to grow?
83761.e: The alpine aster likes sun and dry, stony ground. It often grows on limestone.
83761.m: The alpine aster loves the sun.

83762.q: The word “aster” comes from Greek. What does it mean?
83762.e: “Aster” is Greek for star. The petals stand all around like the rays of a star.

83763.q: How tall does the alpine aster usually grow?
83763.e: The alpine aster is a small plant. It usually grows 5 to 20 centimetres tall.

83764.q: In which kind of garden is the alpine aster often planted?
83764.e: The alpine aster likes stony ground. That is why it suits a rock garden well.
83764.m: Alpine flowers suit a rock garden.

83765.q: Which plant family does the alpine aster belong to?
83765.e: The alpine aster belongs to the daisy family, like the oxeye daisy. Its flower head is made of lots of small single flowers.
83765.m: The alpine aster belongs to the daisy family.

83766.q: How many petals does mountain avens usually have?
83766.e: Mountain avens usually has eight white petals. Its Latin name “octopetala” means “eight petals”.

83767.q: What colour are the petals of mountain avens?
83767.e: Mountain avens has white petals. Lots of yellow stamens stand in the middle.

83768.q: In German, mountain avens is called “silver root”. Why?
a: It is worth as much as silver.
83768.e: The leaves of mountain avens are dark green on top. On the underside they are thickly covered in silvery white hairs.
83768.m: Mountain avens has silvery undersides to its leaves.

a: as a flat carpet on the ground
83769.e: Mountain avens is a dwarf shrub. Its branches creep along the ground and form flat carpets.
83769.m: Mountain avens forms carpets on the ground.

83770.q: What do the fruits of mountain avens have?
83770.e: After flowering, long, feathery hairs grow on the fruits. They look like little silvery tufts.
83770.m: The fruits of mountain avens are feathery.

83771.q: What carries the seeds of mountain avens far away?
83771.e: The seeds have feathery hairs and are very light. So the wind can carry them far.
83771.m: The wind spreads the seeds of mountain avens.

83772.q: What do the leaves of mountain avens remind you of?
83772.e: The leaves of mountain avens have notched edges. They look like tiny oak leaves.
83772.m: Mountain avens has leaves like little oaks.

83773.q: Where does mountain avens often grow?
a: on stony ground in the mountains
83773.e: Mountain avens likes to grow between stones in the mountains. It is one of the first plants to settle on new heaps of stones.

83774.q: What colour are fresh glacier buttercup flowers?
83774.e: The glacier buttercup flowers white at first. Later the colour changes.
83774.m: The glacier buttercup flowers white at first.

83775.q: What happens to glacier buttercup flowers as they get older?
83775.e: Over time the white flowers turn pink and finally dark red. So you often see different colours in one patch.
83775.m: Old glacier buttercup flowers are red.

83776.q: How high up was the glacier buttercup found on the Finsteraarhorn?
83776.e: On the Finsteraarhorn it was found at about 4275 metres. So it grows higher than almost all other flowering plants.
83776.m: The glacier buttercup grows very high up.

83777.e: All kinds of buttercup are poisonous. So you must not eat the glacier buttercup.

83778.q: Where does the glacier buttercup grow?
a: on a lake shore in the valley
83778.e: The glacier buttercup grows on damp scree and bare rock. It often stands very close to the ice, on rock with little lime.
83778.m: The glacier buttercup lives close to the glacier.

83779.q: Which yellow meadow flower is the glacier buttercup closely related to?
83779.e: The meadow buttercup is the yellow buttercup of our meadows. It belongs to the same genus as the glacier buttercup.
83779.m: The glacier buttercup is a relative of the yellow meadow buttercup.

83780.q: Why does the glacier buttercup like to grow under overhanging ice?
a: It is sheltered from the wind there.
There is never any snow there.
83780.e: Under overhanging ice the plant is sheltered from the wind. The ice works like a little greenhouse there.
83780.m: Some plants use the ice like a greenhouse.

83781.q: When does the alpine snowbell flower?
83781.e: The alpine snowbell flowers very early, right at the edge of melting snow. It is one of the first signs of spring in the mountains.
83781.m: The alpine snowbell flowers as the snow melts.

83782.q: What special thing can the alpine snowbell do?
83782.e: The alpine snowbell can grow through a thin layer of snow. The plant makes a little warmth and melts a small hole.
83782.m: The alpine snowbell grows through the snow.

83783.q: What colour is the alpine snowbell usually?
83783.e: The alpine snowbell has blue-violet flowers. They look lovely next to the white snow.

83784.q: What does the edge of the alpine snowbell’s flowers look like?
83784.e: The edge of the little bell is deeply cut. It looks like fine fringes.
83784.m: The alpine snowbell has fringed bells.

83785.q: How do the flowers of the alpine snowbell hang?
83785.e: The little bells of the alpine snowbell hang down. People say they “nod”.
83785.m: The bells of the alpine snowbell nod downwards.

83786.q: What shape are the leaves of the alpine snowbell?
83786.e: The alpine snowbell has small, roundish, leathery leaves. They lie close to the ground.
83786.m: The alpine snowbell has round leaves.

83787.q: Which spring flower is the alpine snowbell related to?
83787.e: The alpine snowbell belongs to the primrose family. The cowslip belongs to it too.
83787.m: The alpine snowbell is a relative of the cowslip.
